title: Leaders Caught As 3 Teams Tie For Top Before Euro Club Cup Final Round
summary: Leaders SuperChess Romania and Novy Bor Chess Club fought out a thrilling draw in round six of the 2026 European Chess Club Cup, with wins for GMs Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Bogdan-Daniel Deac balanced out by wins for GMs Nihal Sarin and David Navara. That enabled top-seed Bayegan Pendik Chess Sports Club to rejoin them in the lead before the final round, after a nerve-wracking 3.5-2.5 win over Tuxera Aquaprofit Nagykanizsai. GMs Amin Tabatabaei and Volodar Murzin more than made up for GM Anish Giri losing on top board to GM Pranesh M. We also have a trio of leaders in the 2026 European Women's Chess Club Cup after fourth-seed CE Gambit Bonnevoie, which had beaten the first, second, and third seeds, finally fell to the fifth—Odlar Yurdu. The match was decided by a single win, for IM Khanim Balajayeva over IM Aleksandra Maltsevskaya, while they were caught by defending champion Cercle d'Echecs de Monte-Carlo, which also relied on a single win—IM Stavroula Tsolakidou's defeat of IM Deimante Daulyte-Cornette. The final round is on Friday, October 23, starting at 8 a.m. ET / 14:00 CEST / 5:30 p.m. IST. There were four wins as the last two remaining perfect teams fought out a 3-3 tie at the top, enabling the Turkish top seed to catch them with a narrow win. Two of the leaders, SuperChess Romania and Bayegan Pendik Chess Sports Club, face off in the final round, while Novy Bor takes on Elektroprivreda, a single point back. Cheddleton, Marseille, and Rishon can also sneak onto the podium with a win, though their tiebreaks likely make gold an impossibility. Open Standings After Round 6 (Top 12) The penultimate round was all we could have hoped for, with incredibly tense battles in the top matches. That was summed up by the battle on top board between the two teams on a perfect 10/10 score. As Abdusattorov described it: "I played against my good friend, my namemate [GM] Nodirbek Yakubboev." Abdusattorov said it was "annoying" to have to play a friend, but on the board neither player held back as Abdusattorov unleashed some sharp home preparation with 11.g4 and Yakubboev responded in kind. The word that Abdusattorov kept returning to was "complicated," but in the end he managed to punish a final mistake and clinch an important win.

title: Wesley So Wins 4th U.S. Chess Championship
summary: GM Wesley So won his fourth national title at the 2026 U.S. Chess Championship after beating the defending champion, GM Fabiano Caruana, 1.5-0.5 in rapid tiebreaks. The previous day played out the least likely scenario: So lost to GM Sam Sevian and Caruana won on demand in his game just to make it to the playoffs. But after a nearly sleepless night, So came back to win his first U.S. Championship in four years and $56,000. As covered in the previous report, WIM Rachael Li won the 2026 U.S. Women's Chess Championship in round 11 without any playoffs. The next world-class event at the Saint Louis Chess Club is the 2026 Clutch Chess Champions Showdown featuring the blockbuster lineup of GMs Javokhir Sindarov, Caruana, Hikaru Nakamura, and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu. The three-day event begins on Tuesday, October 27, at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST. Final Standings | Open So won his first title in 2017, then won again in 2020 and 2021, and four years later he's earned his fourth. This year must be one of the toughest, considering the catastrophe in round 11, but he nevertheless maintained that 2017 was the most difficult as it fielded a 2817-rated Caruana and a 2793-rated Nakamura, as well as a dangerous GM Alex Onischuk, who also played at a 2800+ level in that event as well, according to So. After the last-round loss against Sevian, So said, "I didn't sleep well at all... only two or three hours." Hardly able to put the loss behind him, he was not in the mood to play, but So also gave credit where credit is due. "Kudos to Sam. He had a very tough tournament. I was shocked with the way he played a really good game, but I also played very badly." Kudos to Sam. He had a very tough tournament. —Wesley So on Sam Sevian So commented that this year's championship featured an unusual amount of blunders. He said he was losing against GMs Ray Robson and Jeffery Xiong, but ended up winning both games. The level of play with Caruana in the playoffs was also "very poor quality for both of us. So many blunders and so many mistakes." Both players had just played at the 2026 Chess Olympiad in Uzbekistan before this event, and he said, "In the end, I was really on my last breath. I was literally seeing 10 pawns for Black; my mind was all over the place. But I think Fabi was extremely tired too." It's hard to say who was the moral winner in the draw in game one. So gained a winning advantage with the black pieces in a Nimzo-Indian Defense and could have won on the spot if he had found 34...Qd4+ and 35...Ra1, not a hard combination to spot under normal circumstances—if we may ignore exhaustion and nerves. Caruana went on to save a dead-lost, pawn-down endgame.

title: Moving forward: The global impact of the Intercontinental Online Chess Championship for Prisoners
summary: The 6th Intercontinental Online Chess Championship for Prisoners took place from October 13 to 15, bringing together incarcerated players from around the world for three days of international online competition. This year’s championship established a new participation record, with 140 teams from 56 countries competing. The event was held across men’s, women’s, and youth sections, with teams competing in multiple groups and time zones. Organized by FIDE and the Cook County (Chicago, IL, USA) Sheriff’s Office, the championship demonstrated how chess can be used as an educational and social tool in correctional facilities. Since the first Intercontinental Championship in 2021, the initiative has expanded across six continents, promoting critical thinking, emotional control, teamwork, and skills that support reintegration into society. Let’s take a look at how the “Chess for Freedom” initiative and the recently concluded championship have impacted correctional facilities across the globe. Argentina: A decade of chess Programs in Corrientes correctional facilities For more than ten years, chess programs have been developed in five correctional facilities in the province of Corrientes, Argentina, promoting chess education, training, and competitive opportunities for incarcerated individuals. The strongest players have the opportunity to compete in the tournaments organized inside the prison walls. In addition, some participants who demonstrate a good level of play and good behavior may be allowed to compete in tournaments outside the correctional facilities, provided they receive the necessary judicial and institutional authorizations and appropriate security arrangements are in place. Inmates have access to the internet in the library and to computers for training and competition, with scheduled times to facilitate their participation. This work is part of *Taragüi Koe*, an educational program that provides young people and adults in correctional settings with opportunities to learn and develop skills in different areas. Within this framework, Professor Franco Penelli and I, Samuel Gogna, a physical education teacher and chess coach, focus on teaching and promoting chess. Over the years, several students have achieved a strong competitive level. Many who have been released continue to participate in tournaments outside the correctional system. The program coordinators maintain contact with them, share information about upcoming competitions, and encourage them to remain connected to the chess community. Romania: A staple of the Online Chess Championship for Prisoners The Romanian penitentiary system participated in the Intercontinental Online Chess Championship for Prisoners for the fifth consecutive time. Romania was represented by two men’s teams, one women’s team and one youth team, comprising prisoners from 14 penitentiary institutions across the country. The Romanian teams demonstrated a strong competitive spirit and achieved noteworthy results throughout the championship. Beyond sporting performance, participation in this international event provided an opportunity to promote important values such as discipline, strategic thinking, patience, and respect for rules and fair play. The experience gained through successive participations in the Intercontinental Championship also inspired the Romanian National Administration of Penitentiaries to develop its own national online chess competition for prisoners. In 2026, this initiative reached its second edition, reflecting a growing commitment to promoting chess as an educational and recreational activity within the penitentiary system. The national competition provides prisoners from different penitentiary institutions with the opportunity to test their skills, develop their abilities and engage in constructive competition, while also encouraging greater participation in future international events. Through these initiatives, the Romanian National Administration of Penitentiaries continues to promote chess not only as a competitive sport but also as a valuable tool for personal development, social interaction and preparation for reintegration into society. Ghana: Expanding the “Chess for Freedom” initiative in prisons Following the success of the Chess for Freedom initiative with Ghana’s Youth at the Senior Correctional Centre in Accra, Mentors Chess Academy, in partnership with the Ghana Prisons Service, expanded the programme to Nsawam Male Prison and Nsawam Female Prison in 2025. Over the past year, the initiative has used chess to promote discipline, patience, critical thinking, confidence and positive personal development among inmates in both facilities. Earlier this year, the male and female teams participated in the African Continental Online Chess Championship for Prisoners, gaining valuable competitive experience and representing Ghana in the continental event. Through regular chess sessions, participants are developing their skills, building connections and discovering new opportunities for personal growth. The encouraging response from inmates and prison officers reinforces our belief that chess can play a valuable role in rehabilitation and support the reintegration of inmates into society. Australia: Karnet Prison Farm, WA, makes its meaningful debut A team from Karnet Prison Farm, WA, Australia, debuted in the 6th Intercontinental Online Chess Championship for Prisoners. While the team did not manage to advance to the semifinals, the outcomes demonstrate the considerable potential of chess as a rehabilitative, educational and reintegration tool across our correctional facilities. Over the two months preceding the tournament, eight prisoners from various accommodation units at Karnet committed to preparing for the tournament, participating in twice-weekly chess sessions. The participants were selected by a prisoner who had taken a leadership role in coordinating the group, ensuring that each man had the opportunity to contribute and develop his skills. On the first group stage, Karnet secured eight victories from its 28 games against Philippines, India, Mongolia, United Arab Emirates and Singapore – a commendable achievement for our first international competition. What unfolded over the four and a half hours on the group stage was far more significant than a chess tournament. As the first games commenced, the silence in the room was extraordinary. You could quite literally have heard a pin drop. Eight men from different units, with different backgrounds, experiences and offending histories, sat together with a common purpose. There was no competition for attention, no unnecessary conversation, and no frustration when a game did not go their way. Instead, there was concentration, encouragement, cooperation, and an unmistakable sense of shared achievement. The men patiently awaited their turns, supported one another, discussed strategies when appropriate, and demonstrated genuine respect for everyone’s opportunity to compete. title: European Club Cup: Three co-leaders in both sections going into final round
summary:
Three teams share the lead in both sections of the European Club Cup ahead of Friday's final round. In the open, SuperChess and Novy Bor drew their direct encounter, allowing Bayegan Pendik to catch up with a narrow victory over Tuxera Aquaprofit Nagykanizsai. In the women's competition, Gambit Bonnevoie suffered their first defeat, leaving Monte-Carlo and Odlar Yurdu level with the Luxembourg club. | Pictured: Bayegan Pendik's Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus | Photo: Gerd Densing

Open: Contested matches at the top

Three teams share first place in the open section of the European Club Cup following Thursday's sixth (and penultimate) round in Budva.

Defending champions SuperChess Romania and Novy Bor Chess Club drew their direct encounter 3–3, allowing top seeds Bayegan Pendik Chess Sports Club to catch them with a narrow 3½–2½ victory over Tuxera Aquaprofit Nagykanizsai.

All three teams enter the final round with 11/12 match points, while four clubs remain in contention for medals with 10 points.

Sveti Stefan, a small island connected to the mainland by a narrow tombolo, is situated approximately 6 kilometres (3.7 mi) southeast of Budva - Bobby Fischer and Boriss Spassky played the first 11 games of their 1992 rematch on the island | Photo: Gerd Densing

The encounter between SuperChess and Novy Bor featured four decisive games, with both teams holding the advantage at different stages. On the top board, Nodirbek Abdusattorov defeated his namesake and teammate Nodirbek Yakubboev to give the Romanian club an important point. Nihal Sarin responded by beating Jorden van Foreest on board two.

Bogdan-Daniel Deac subsequently put SuperChess ahead by defeating Nils Grandelius, while David Navara overcame Daniel Dardha on the sixth board to restore equality. Notably, Dardha came from winning all five of his previous games in Budva. The remaining two encounters ended drawn.

Novy Bor v. SuperChess | Photo: Gerd Densing

SuperChess 3-3 Novy Bor

Select an entry from the list to switch between games

While the top match saw the co-leaders split the match points, Bayegan Pendik secured a crucial victory over fifth seeds Tuxera Aquaprofit Nagykanizsai. The Turkish representatives overcame an individual defeat on the top board, where Indian grandmaster Pranesh M defeated Anish Giri. It was Giri's second loss in four appearances at the tournament.

Victories by Amin Tabatabaei against Andrei Volokitin and Volodar Murzin against Maksim Chigaev proved sufficient for Bayegan Pendik to win the match.

Anish Giri and Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus playing on the top two boards for Bayegan Pendik | Photo: Gerd Densing

Tuxera Aquaprofit Nagykanizsai 2½-3½ Bayegan Pendik

Elektroprivreda, the sixth seeds, missed an opportunity to join the leaders after being held to a 3–3 draw by second seeds Alkaloid. Elektroprivreda, representing Montenegro, nevertheless remain just one match point behind the leading trio. They are joined on 10/12 by Rishon LeZion A, Marseille Echecs and Cheddleton Savills Caterling.

Friday's final round will see Bayegan Pendik face SuperChess in a direct encounter between two of the leaders, while Novy Bor take on Elektroprivreda. Cheddleton will meet Rishon LeZion A, while Marseille Echecs face Alkaloid.

Arjun Erigaisi, Wei Yi (not in the photo) and Yu Yangyi lead Alkaloid, the second seeds in Budva | Photo: Gerd Densing

Women's: Gambit Bonnevoie suffer first loss

The women's competition also has three teams tied for first place ahead of Friday's final round. CE Gambit Bonnevoie, who had won all five of their previous matches, suffered their first defeat against fifth seeds Odlar Yurdu, while defending champions Cercle d'Echecs de Monte-Carlo narrowly defeated SuperChess Romania.

The results leave all three teams on 10/12 match points, with Sirmium Sremska Mitrovica, Crvena Zvezda and Davit Jojua's Chess Club following on 8/12. Since none of the co-leaders face each other (they have already played each other in previous rounds), the three chasers have a very small theoretical chance of creating a six-way tie at the top if all three score wins.

The penultimate round in progress | Photo: Gerd Densing

Gambit Bonnevoie entered the sixth round with a two-point advantage over their closest pursuers, having already defeated the three highest-rated teams in the competition. However, the Luxembourg-based club could not extend their winning streak against Azerbaijan's Odlar Yurdu, who secured a 2½–1½ victory.

The decisive point came on the fourth board, where Khanim Balajayeva defeated Aleksandra Maltsevskaya. The remaining three games ended in draws. The victory allowed Odlar Yurdu to catch their opponents in the standings.

Anna Ushenina facing Ulviyya Fataliyeva on the top board | Photo: Gerd Densing

Monte-Carlo joined the leading group by defeating third seeds SuperChess Romania 2½–1½. Stavroula Tsolakidou scored the only victory of the match, beating Deimante Daulyte-Cornette on board three.

The encounter was particularly demanding for Monte-Carlo on the remaining boards. Cramling managed to save a difficult position against Marsel Efroimski, while Humpy Koneru defended a pawn-down endgame against Dinara Wagner in a 95-move game. Koneru finally secured the half-point that gave her team the match victory.

Monte-Carlo's Aleksandra Goryachkina and Humpy Koneru | Photo: Gerd Densing

Monte-Carlo 2½-1½ SuperChess

Elsewhere, 11-year-old English star Bodhana Sivanandan recorded her fourth individual win in Budva, defeating Arina Budiak of Klaipeda. Representing She Plays To Win Lionesses A, Sivanandan has collected 4½/6 points, with her only defeat coming against Aleksandra Goryachkina (the highest-rated player in the field) in the opening round.

The final round will see Monte-Carlo face 15 th seeds Davit Jojua's Chess Club, while Odlar Yurdu take on second seeds Sirmium Sremska Mitrovica. Gambit Bonnevoie will meet seventh seeds Crvena Zvezda. As mentioned above, none of the three leaders will face each other.

title: Rachel Li wins US Women's Championship on her debut
summary:
Going into the final round of the 2026 US Women’s Championship in St Louis, Rachael Li was the sole leader with 8 points from 10 games, one point ahead of Alice Lee. Li therefore needed only a draw against Anna Zatonskih in the final round to win the tournament. Li secured both the draw and the title, becoming US Women's Champion at just 16 years of age. She also collected $45,000 in prize money, qualified for the next Women's World Cup and earned her first IM norm. | Photo: Lennart Ootes / Saint Louis Chess Club

The first player to take the title on her debut

Rachel Li and Anna Zatonskih drew after 49 moves in an opposite-coloured bishop endgame, but the game could very nearly have ended shortly after it began. Zatonskih had the opportunity to force a draw by threefold repetition after only 14 moves, but as she explained during the game in the "Confessional", she would have considered that "unfair to Alice Lee".

Li therefore won the title in her very first appearance at the US Women's Championship and became the youngest player to do so on her debut. The youngest US women's champion of all time, however, remains Irina Krush, who won her first title at the age of 14.

Irina Krush during her game against Tatev Abrahamyan | Photo: Crystal Fuller

After the game, Li thanked above all her older brother, grandmaster Ruifeng Li, who had helped her with her preparation. She also thanked her parents: "They were more nervous during the tournament than I was".

Alice Lee interviewed by Maurice Ashley

For her success, Li received $45,000 in prize money: $35,000 for first place, a $5,000 winner's bonus and a further $5,000 for the "Finish Strong Prize", a special award for the best result over the final six rounds.

Alice Lee defeated Anna Sargsyan and finished clear second, one point behind, earning $30,000 in prize money and qualification for the next Women's World Cup.

Alice Lee | Photo: Crystal Fuller

Krush finished third after defeating Abrahamyan in the final round. Rose Atwell produced an attractive combination in the last round, defeating Nazi Paikidze with a queen sacrifice.

title: US Championship 2026: Tiebreak!
summary:
The 2026 U.S. Championship came to a dramatic conclusion: Wesley So lost to last-placed Sam Sevian in the final round, ending his 48-game unbeaten streak at the U.S. Championships. Fabiano Caruana, meanwhile, won on demand against Awonder Liang to catch So at the top of the standings. The title will now be decided in a playoff, beginning with two rapid games at 15+10. If the scores remain level, another two rapid games will follow, then up to two two-game blitz matches at 5+2. If the players are still tied, the arbiter will decide how to proceed. | Live with commentary from 12.00 CDT / 18.00 BST / 19.00 CEST | Photo: Crystal Fuller

Old Rivals

Wesley So and Fabiano Caruana have played numerous games against each other, including in tiebreaks. In classical chess, Caruana has the better head-to-head record, with 8 wins, 5 losses and 34 draws (including the current championship). In rapid and blitz chess, however, their records are remarkably close. In rapid, So leads by 15 wins to 14, with 23 draws, while in blitz, Caruana has a narrow lead of 17 wins to 16, with 19 draws.

The two are no strangers to playoffs, either. At the 2020 Clutch Chess Champions Showdown, So prevailed after a 9-9 tie thanks to the special scoring system used for the so-called clutch games. At the 2025 Sinquefield Cup, Caruana and So faced Praggnanandhaa in a three-player blitz playoff. So won the tiebreak and the tournament.

At the Grand Chess Tour Finals in August, Caruana defeated So in the semifinals, while So came out on top at the American Cup in St. Louis. There is therefore no clear favourite going into today's playoff.

title: All new releases in September!
summary:
The latest releases offer fresh ideas for opening preparation and regular chess training. In two volumes, Michael Kotyk presents a practical repertoire for Black after 1.e4 e5, while Fabien Libiszewski introduces the dynamic Chigorin Defence against the Queen's Gambit. ChessBase Magazine 233 rounds off the selection with up-to-date opening ideas, annotated games by top players and a wide range of training material. The products combine practical recommendations for tournament play with suggestions for independent analysis. | All photos: ChessBase

New releases: September 2026

Surprise Weapons Against 1.e4 – Volume 1

In the first part of his repertoire for Black after 1.e4 e5, Michael Kotyk focuses on the open games arising after 2.Nf3 Nc6. The main topics include the Scotch Game and the Scotch Gambit, the Centre Game, the Vienna Game and the Four Knights Game.

Rather than concentrating exclusively on established main lines, Kotyk favours dynamic variations and less familiar move orders that are well suited to practical tournament preparation. Examples such as the Scotch Gambit with 4.Bc4 Nf6 5.e5 d5 illustrate his active approach.

Surprise Weapons Against 1.e4 – Volume 2

In Volume 2, Michael Kotyk completes his repertoire. He covers the King's Gambit, the Centre Game, the Italian Game and the Ruy Lopez. Here, too, the emphasis is on active options and variations with practical surprise value.

In the King's Gambit, for example, Kotyk examines 2...Bc5, while in the Ruy Lopez he presents, among other things, unusual approaches against White's classical setups. Together with Volume 1, this provides a comprehensive repertoire for players who want to fight for the initiative with 1...e5.

The Chigorin Defence: A Practical Weapon Against the Queen's Gambit

Fabien Libiszewski presents an active alternative to established systems against the Queen's Gambit. After 1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6, Black focuses on development and immediate counterplay against White's centre, while accepting certain structural concessions.

The course explains the most important continuations, including 3.e3, 3.Nc3 and 3.Nf3, as well as setups such as the London System and the Catalan. Model games by players such as Morozevich and Rapport illustrate the possibilities.
